questions.question: What is a user in Linux?

options.text: A physical person using a computer
An account that allows a person or process to log in and use system resources
A file that stores system settings
A running process in memory

explanation.correct: A Linux user is an account — it can represent a real person or an automated process — that the OS uses to control access to system resources.
explanation.why: A is incorrect because system users represent processes, not people. C and D describe other OS components.

questions.question: What is the UID of the root user in Linux?

explanation.correct: The root user always has UID 0. This is hardcoded — the kernel uses UID 0 to identify the superuser regardless of the username.
explanation.why: UID 1 and UID 100 are system user ranges. UID 1000 is where normal user accounts typically start on modern Linux.

questions.question: Which file stores encrypted user passwords in Linux?

options.text: /etc/passwd
/etc/users
/etc/shadow
/etc/auth

explanation.correct: /etc/shadow stores encrypted (hashed) passwords and is readable only by root. /etc/passwd is world-readable but only stores an 'x' as a password placeholder.
explanation.why: /etc/passwd was the original location but was insecure because it is world-readable. /etc/users and /etc/auth do not exist.

questions.question: What UID range is typically assigned to normal users on modern Linux systems?

options.text: 1000 and above

explanation.correct: On modern Linux distributions (RHEL 7+, Ubuntu 16+), normal user accounts start at UID 1000.
explanation.why: UID 0 is root. UIDs 1–999 are reserved for system users/service accounts. 500–999 was the old RHEL range.

questions.question: What does 'sudo' stand for?

options.text: Super User Directory Override
Switch User, Do
Superuser Do
System User Daemon Operations

explanation.correct: sudo stands for 'superuser do'. It allows an authorised user to execute a command as the superuser (root) or another user.
explanation.why: The other options are common myths or misrememberings.

questions.question: What does the 'x' in the permission string -rwxr-xr-- mean in the owner's position?

options.text: The file is executable by the owner
The file is encrypted
The owner has been excluded
The file is a special system file

explanation.correct: The 'x' in the owner position (characters 2-4) means the file owner has execute permission — they can run this file as a program.
explanation.why: Encryption and special file types are indicated differently. 'x' always and only means execute permission.

questions.question: What numeric value does 'write' (w) represent in octal permission notation?

explanation.correct: In Linux permission notation: read=4, write=2, execute=1. These add up to create any combination (e.g., rwx = 4+2+1 = 7).
explanation.why: 4 is read, 1 is execute, 8 is not used. This is a fundamental fact that must be memorised.

questions.question: Which file controls which users are allowed to use sudo?

options.text: /etc/group
/etc/sudoers
/etc/passwd
/etc/sudo.conf

explanation.correct: /etc/sudoers is the configuration file that lists which users and groups can use sudo, and which commands they are allowed to run.
explanation.why: /etc/group manages group memberships but not sudo privileges. /etc/passwd stores user details. /etc/sudo.conf is not the main authorisation file.

questions.question: What is the default home directory for the root user?

options.text: /home/root
/usr/root
/root
/var/root

explanation.correct: The root user's home directory is /root (not /home/root). All other users' home directories are under /home/username.
explanation.why: This is a common exam trap. Root does not follow the /home/ convention — it has its own top-level /root directory.

questions.question: What does the chmod command do?

options.text: Changes file ownership
Changes file permissions
Changes the current directory
Creates a new user

explanation.correct: chmod (change mode) changes the read, write, and execute permissions on files and directories.
explanation.why: chown changes ownership. cd changes directory. useradd creates users. Each command has its own distinct purpose.

questions.question: What permission string does chmod 755 create?

options.text: rwxr--r--
rwxrwxr-x
rwxr-xr-x
rw-r-xr-x

explanation.correct: 7=rwx (owner), 5=r-x (group), 5=r-x (others). So chmod 755 produces rwxr-xr-x. This is the standard permission for directories and scripts.
explanation.why: 755 = 7(rwx) + 5(r-x) + 5(r-x). You must calculate each digit: 4+2+1=7, 4+0+1=5, 4+0+1=5.

questions.question: What is a GID?

options.text: Global Instance Directory
Group Identity Document
Group ID — a unique numeric identifier for a Linux group
Guest ID used for anonymous access

explanation.correct: GID stands for Group ID — it is the unique numeric identifier the Linux kernel uses internally to track group membership and permissions.
explanation.why: The kernel does not use group names internally — it uses GIDs. This mirrors how UIDs work for users.

questions.question: A user runs 'cat /etc/shadow' and gets 'Permission denied'. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: The file is encrypted and cannot be read
The user is a normal user without root privileges — /etc/shadow is root-only
The file does not exist on this system
The cat command cannot read shadow files

explanation.correct: /etc/shadow is protected so that only root (or processes with root privileges via sudo) can read it. A normal user always gets Permission denied.
explanation.why: The file exists on every Linux system. cat can read any file the user has permission for. The file contains password hashes, not encrypted data.

questions.question: What does 'usermod -aG sudo alice' do?

options.text: Removes alice from the sudo group
Replaces all of alice's groups with sudo
Appends alice to the sudo group without removing her from existing groups
Creates a new sudo group and adds alice

explanation.correct: The -aG flag means 'append to Group'. It adds alice to the sudo group while keeping all her existing group memberships intact.
explanation.why: Using just -G without -a would replace all existing groups — a dangerous mistake. -aG is the safe way to add to a group.

questions.question: What is a primary group in Linux?

options.text: The most important group on the system
The group automatically created with the same name as the user when the user account is created
The administrators group
A group the admin manually assigns to each user

explanation.correct: When you create a user in Linux, a primary group with the same name as the username is automatically created. The user is placed in this group by default.
explanation.why: There is no automatic 'most important' or 'admin' group. The primary group is simply the default group assigned at account creation.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the SUID permission bit?

options.text: Allows any user to delete the file
Makes the file run with the permissions of the file's owner, not the user executing it
Prevents the file from being deleted even by root
Makes the file readable by all users on the system

explanation.correct: SUID (Set User ID) causes a program to run with its owner's privileges. Classic example: /usr/bin/passwd runs as root (its owner) so any user can update passwords in /etc/shadow.
explanation.why: SUID does not affect deletion or readability. The sticky bit prevents deletion by non-owners. No permission prevents root from deleting.

questions.question: What does the sticky bit do when set on a directory like /tmp?

options.text: The directory cannot be deleted
Only the file owner, directory owner, or root can delete files within it
All files created inside are executable
The directory is hidden from ls output

explanation.correct: The sticky bit on a directory means users can create and read files, but only the file's owner, the directory owner, or root can delete or rename files inside it.
explanation.why: This is why /tmp (chmod 1777) allows everyone to create files but prevents users from deleting each other's temporary files.

questions.question: What is the correct way to open and edit /etc/sudoers safely?

options.text: nano /etc/sudoers
vi /etc/sudoers
sudo visudo
sudo cat /etc/sudoers > /tmp/edit.txt

explanation.correct: visudo is the only safe way to edit /etc/sudoers. It validates syntax before saving, preventing you from locking yourself out due to a typo.
explanation.why: Editing sudoers directly with nano or vi is dangerous — a syntax error can permanently break sudo access with no way to fix it without root login.

questions.question: What does 'userdel -r alice' do differently from 'userdel alice'?

options.text: Recursively deletes all files alice ever created system-wide
Deletes alice's account AND her home directory and mail spool
Only removes alice from all groups
Forces deletion even if alice is currently logged in

explanation.correct: The -r flag (remove) deletes the user account AND removes their home directory (/home/alice) and mail spool. Without -r, the home directory is left behind.
explanation.why: It does not delete all files system-wide — only the home directory. Use 'find / -user alice' to find files elsewhere if needed.

questions.question: A file has permissions rw-r--r-- (644). A user in the file's group tries to write to it. What happens?

options.text: The write succeeds because group members always inherit owner permissions
The write is denied — group permissions are r-- (read only)
The write succeeds only if the user uses sudo
The system prompts for a password before allowing the write

explanation.correct: In 644 (rw-r--r--): owner has rw, group has r-- (read only), others have r--. A group member can only read the file, not write to it.
explanation.why: Group members use the middle three bits (positions 5-7). With r--, they have read permission only. Sudo would bypass permissions but was not specified.

questions.question: What does the SGID bit do when set on a directory?

options.text: Only the directory owner can create files inside it
New files created inside inherit the directory's group ownership
All files inside the directory execute with group privileges
The directory becomes invisible to users not in the group

explanation.correct: SGID on a directory ensures that any file created inside it inherits the directory's group, not the creating user's primary group. Ideal for shared team directories.
explanation.why: SUID (not SGID) affects execution privileges. SGID on directories is specifically about group inheritance for new files.

questions.question: The default umask on most Linux systems is 022. What permissions will a newly created file have?

explanation.correct: Files have a max of 666. 666 - 022 = 644 (rw-r--r--). The umask subtracts from the maximum to give the default permission.
explanation.why: Directories get 777 - 022 = 755. Files cannot have 777 by default because the execute bit is not in the file maximum of 666.

questions.question: What is the difference between /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow?

options.text: /etc/passwd has user info and is world-readable; /etc/shadow has hashed passwords and is root-only
They contain identical information in different formats
/etc/shadow is for system users; /etc/passwd is for normal users
/etc/passwd is newer and replaces /etc/shadow on modern systems

explanation.correct: /etc/passwd contains general user info (username, UID, GID, home directory, shell) and is world-readable. /etc/shadow contains the actual hashed passwords and is only accessible by root.
explanation.why: Shadow passwords were introduced specifically because /etc/passwd is world-readable — storing hashed passwords there was a security vulnerability.

questions.question: On Amazon Linux, which group membership allows ec2-user to use sudo?

options.text: sudo
root
admin
wheel

explanation.correct: On Amazon Linux (and RHEL/CentOS-based systems), the wheel group is granted sudo privileges in /etc/sudoers. The ec2-user is a member of wheel by default.
explanation.why: The 'sudo' group is the equivalent on Debian/Ubuntu systems. 'root' is a user, not a group. 'admin' is not the standard on Amazon Linux.

questions.question: What command shows all groups a user belongs to?

options.text: userinfo username
cat /etc/group | grep username
groups username
id --groups username

explanation.correct: 'groups username' directly shows all group memberships for that user. 'id' also shows this (as part of more output) and is also correct but C is the most direct answer.
explanation.why: userinfo is not a standard command. grep on /etc/group only finds groups where the user is listed as a secondary member, missing the primary group entry.

questions.question: A web server process needs to read files in /var/www/html, but those files are owned by root:root with permissions 640. The web server runs as user 'www-data'. What is the best fix?

options.text: chmod 777 /var/www/html
chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/html
Run the web server as root
Set the SUID bit on the web server binary

explanation.correct: The correct fix is to change ownership to www-data so the web server process (running as www-data) has owner-level access. Keep permissions at 640 or 644 for security.
explanation.why: chmod 777 is dangerously insecure. Running services as root violates least privilege and is a major security risk. SUID on the binary creates a different kind of security hole.

questions.question: You need to give a user temporary root access for one command without adding them to sudoers permanently. What is the safest approach?

options.text: Give them the root password
Add them to sudoers with NOPASSWD:ALL permanently
Use 'sudo -u root command' from an already-authorised user account
Add a time-limited sudo rule in /etc/sudoers.d/ for specific commands only

explanation.correct: Best practice is to create a targeted sudoers rule allowing only the specific command needed, placed in /etc/sudoers.d/ for easy management and removal. This follows the principle of least privilege.
explanation.why: Sharing the root password removes accountability. NOPASSWD:ALL is overly broad. Option C requires another authorised user to be present.

questions.question: What does 'chmod 4755 /usr/bin/myapp' do?

options.text: Sets sticky bit with rwxr-xr-x
Sets SUID bit — myapp runs as its owner regardless of who executes it
Sets SGID bit — myapp inherits the group of the directory
Makes the file immutable — no one can change permissions

explanation.correct: The leading 4 in 4755 sets the SUID bit. Combined with 755 (rwxr-xr-x), any user can execute myapp but it runs with the file owner's permissions — common for tools like passwd.
explanation.why: Sticky bit is leading 1 (1xxx). SGID is leading 2 (2xxx). There is no chmod option for immutability — that requires chattr.

questions.question: A developer needs to collaborate on files in /project/ with another developer. New files must automatically belong to the 'devs' group. What is the correct setup?

options.text: chmod 777 /project/
Set SUID on /project/
Set SGID on /project/ with chmod g+s or chmod 2770
Edit /etc/group to add devs as the owner of /project/

explanation.correct: SGID on a directory makes all new files inherit the directory's group. Combined with chown :devs /project and chmod 2770, both developers can work in the directory and all files automatically belong to 'devs'.
explanation.why: SUID on a directory has no effect. 777 is insecure and does not fix the group inheritance problem. /etc/group tracks membership, not file ownership.

questions.question: An attacker gains read access to /etc/shadow. Why is this serious even though passwords are hashed?

options.text: It is not serious — hashed passwords are completely safe
The attacker can reverse the hash directly using a simple algorithm
The attacker can use offline brute-force or dictionary attacks against the hashes
The attacker can read the hash and use it directly as a password (pass-the-hash)

explanation.correct: While password hashes cannot be reversed directly, an attacker with the hash file can run offline attacks — testing millions of password guesses per second against the hash using tools like hashcat or john — until they find a match.
explanation.why: Modern hashes (SHA-512 with salt) cannot be reversed directly. Pass-the-hash works on NTLM (Windows) but not on Linux shadow hashes. This is why /etc/shadow must remain root-only.
